## Code

Everything public lives in one repository: [github.com/hungshinlee/Speech-AI](https://github.com/hungshinlee/Speech-AI) (the GitHub icon in the top-right corner goes there too).

- **Slides** — `slides/wNN.qmd`, rendered at [Slides](slides.qmd). They are Quarto reveal.js decks; the source is readable as Markdown.
- **Analysis scripts referenced on the slides** — `slides/scripts/`, e.g. [`analyze_duplex_audio.py`](slides/scripts/analyze_duplex_audio.py) (energy VAD, overlap / response / stop latency) and [`make_duplex_timeline.py`](slides/scripts/make_duplex_timeline.py) (two-track timeline). Standard library + `numpy`/`scipy`/`matplotlib`; run them on any stereo WAV with the user on the left channel and the system on the right.
- **Weekly pages** are generated from the course outline; the outline itself is not published.

## Practical Notes on the Demos

The demos are run live in class by the lecturer on the machine described above; you do not need to set anything up. Three things about them are worth knowing:

- The first weight download and the first Metal / Core ML compile often take longer than the inference itself, so every model is loaded and warmed up before class. If a demo is played back from a rehearsal recording instead of run live, the screen says so.
- A few dozen utterances from LibriSpeech `dev-clean` plus MUSAN are enough for everything shown; nothing needs a large dataset.
- The six "play the broken one first" demos are the most memorable part of the course: Griffin-Lim phase reconstruction (W2), the CTC blank posterior heatmap (W3), Whisper hallucination (W7), vocoder artifacts (W8), WER going *up* after enhancement (W10), and barging in versus responding too slowly (W12).
